newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Labour says NZ First IR policy no obstacle to deal.
newsitem.headline: Labour says NZ First IR policy no obstacle to deal.

text.p: Labour leader Helen Clark on Thursday described New Zealand First's industrial relations policy a "damp squib, light on detail and essentially incoherent" but said it left room for negotiation after the election.
"The policy is so insubstantial that it seems to leave considerable ground for negotiation within a Labour-led government after October 12," Clark said.

But she was critical of New Zealand First's decision to retain the current law making strikes and lock-outs related to multi-employer documents illegal, as was the Alliance's industrial relations spokeswoman Laila Harre.
A general election is due on October 12, and on current polling a combination of Labour, New Zealand First and the Alliance could oust the ruling National Party.
Clark said New Zealand First's policy on good faith bargaining was "certainly compatible with Labour policy, as is the provision for better access for workers' representatives to worksites".

"The refusal to meet International Labour Organisation provisions on the right to strike, however, will be a major point of concern. Nor is widespread compulsory arbitration something that either workers or employers are looking for," Clark said.
The Alliance's Harre told Reuters New Zealand First's position on strikes for multi-employer documents was fundamentally incompatible with Labour's position.
"I want to know which will trade away their policy after the election."
She said the New Zealand First policy released by its deputy leader Tau Hanare was light on content because the party supported the Employment Contracts Act.

"Tau Henare has spent three years more than he should in Parliament. He has lost touch. His policies do not resolve the fundamental problem of using divided workplaces to drive down wages and conditions over time."
She said he had clearly not read the ILO's criticism of the ban on strikes.
"New Zealand First' means New Zealand only' when it comes to legal arrangements," she said.
